items.title: Akiyoshi Toshiko — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I still have, heavily, I have a lot of influence from Bud Powell

ctx.x: Yugoslavia. So things like that had a lot to do with it. But also his music, you know, he was … more, becoming more, more and more like a universal [??], so on. I realized my thinking was so shallow, and so…. He really um … highly … thought of me as, some of the music that I have, like “Kogun,” for example, or “Minamata”…. You know, he actually used “Kogun” as material, teaching material at Harvard when he was teaching [in the] summer. I have nothing but fond memories, and then I have … today, you know, I have, I…
Well, you brought up two very important, uh, uh, things that we should try to discuss in more detail. One is influence, you know, what you were saying is, looking at cultural influences in music….

items.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: This is when I got very much into Bud Powell.

ctx.x: Did you start writing them down, or did they just become memorized immediately yourself?

At one time I used to write out everything. I remember I had quite a lot of standards a long time ago, like 78 records. But most of the time, much later I just played a number of them. This is when I got very much into Bud Powell. And after that I think I would just

play his record and I just learned how to play like that. And by that time I had my little piano so mostly, most of the memorization was later on. First, early days, I used to copy it and put it on a tape.
